title: Feeding behavior and mechanics of sharks: past, present and future

authors.affiliation: Department of Biology, University of South Florida, 4202 East Fowler Ave., Tampa, Florida, 33620 U.S.A.

abstract_text: Knowledge of the feeding behavior of sharks is based on a rich history of descriptive studies, and understanding of the feeding mechanism is rooted in anatomy. These works posed as many questions as they answered. Questions about the feeding mechanism and the function of jaw protrusion remain, the degree of stereotypy of prey capture behavior, the role of jaw suspension in feeding, and how a relatively simple morphological system evolved to the current diversity of feeding forms. Research is now addressing these questions. Utilizing anatomical techniques, computer imaging, electromyography and kinematic analysis, models of the feeding apparatus are being proposed. Prey capture behavior appears not to be a modal action pattern, many sharks exhibiting variability and modulatory abilities. Jaw suspension is not clearly related to feeding behavior as was once thought, and our work has revealed evolutionary shifts that influenced the diversity of feeding forms. We are now posed with additional questions of the evolution of suction feeding and the scaling of prey capture kinematics. The feeding behavior and mechanics of elasmobranchs continue to be an exciting and relatively unexplored area that promises to further our understanding of these apex predators and augment our knowledge of lower vertebrate feeding mechanisms.

title: Preference for static and dynamic criteria in Physalaemus pustulosus

abstract_text: Anuran call properties were classified as static or dynamic based on within-male variability during bouts of calling. Females exert stabilizing or weakly directional selection on static properties, and highly directional selection on dynamic properties. Selection pressure was examined in two call characteristics; a static character (dominant frequency of the whine), and one dynamic character (intervals between whines). Six phonotaxis experiments were conducted with gravid females using synthetic calls. Stimuli presented for both characters are based on the mean and standard deviation of those characters in the study population, to compare preferences between static and dynamic characters. For each character, 3 distinct intervals of variation have been used (1SD, 2SD, and 3SD), that which is translated in 3 different experiments: mean-1.5SD vs. mean-0.5SD, mean-1.5SD vs. mean+0.5SD and mean-1.5SD vs. mean+1.5SD. As expected, preference was strong in the dynamic character, increasing in proportion to the increase in the interval between stimuli. Preference for the static character remained constant. The degree of 'motivation' in the choice made by females was measured as the time taken to make the choice, the number of speakers visited, and the number of females necessary to get 20 valid responses. For both characters an increase in female 'motivation' was observed in proportion to the increase in the interval of variation between stimuli. Furthermore, all these measures of 'motivation' were greater in the dynamic character than the static character.

title: Acoustic competition in Physalaemus pustulosus, a differential response to calls of relative frequency

abstract_text: The response of male Physalaemus pustulosus to conspecific whines of different frequencies was examined. In the first block of playback experiments (fixed response), three types of synthetic stimuli (HFR, MFR, LFR) were used that corresponded to calls of high frequency (mean+2 SD), mid-frequency (mean), and low frequency (mean-2 SD) for the study population. In the second block of interactive playback experiments (relative response) whines of relative frequency to that of the male subject were used: male frequency + 2 SD (HRR), male frequency (MRR), and male frequency - 2 SD (LRR). In the fixed frequency experiments, no modification of male vocal response was observed. However, in the relative frequency experiments, males responded with greater rates of whine production, and above all, with more complex calls (adding secondary notes) to stimuli of similar or higher frequency than to stimuli of lower frequency than their own. In other words, male vocal competition is greater only when competitors have similar or relatively higher whine frequencies to their own, and does not increase when competitors have call frequencies which are at the mean or higher for the population as a whole. Nevertheless, this differential response cannot be explained only as an effect of competition between males of different sizes, given that the relationship between frequency of the whine and male size is very weak.

title: The agonistic behaviors of the blackbanded sunfish Enneacanthus chaetodon

abstract_text: The Blackbanded sunfish (Enneacanthus chaetodon) could be considered a cosmopolitan species of the Atlantic coastline (except in Virginia and Maryland, where they are an endangered species). E. chaetodon prefers calm lentic waters which are highly vegetated and extremely acidic in nature. This species quickly adapts to captivity and readily shows aggressive behaviors at low densities. The experiment was designed to determine if the onset of agonistic behaviors in E. chaetodon was significantly influenced by size, density, and/or time. Research has indicated that the encroachment of inter individual space and the acclimation period (a function of time) were both shown to be a significant factor for the onset of aggression. Size, however, was not considered a significant factor for the onset of aggression. The onset of submissive behaviors were considered significant related to the relative body size and with the encroachment of inter individual space; yet it was not considered significant in relation to time. The results indicate that the changes in the agonistic behaviors of E. chaetodon occur as a function of time, encounter, and density.

abstract_text: Variation in temperature and hydration may significantly affect the jumping performance of amphibians and therefore their foraging efficiency, habitat selection, survivorship and fitness. Jumping performance (maximum jumping distance) was measured at three temperatures (20°C, 25°C and 30°C) and two hydration levels (100% and 75%). E. antillensis showed a significant decrease in jumping ability under dehydration condition at 25°C and 30°C. However at 20°C, there was no significant decrease in jumping ability for E. antillensis. E. cochranae showed no differences in jumping ability. E. cochranae seems to have greater tolerance to changes in temperature and hydration.

title: Response of ravine salamanders to chemical stimuli from autonomized tails

abstract_text: The ability to detect chemical cues is an important predator avoidance mechanism in many organisms, which is best known in aquatic organisms. Only a few studies have examined this ability in terrestrial salamanders. In this experiment, I investigated the response (i.e., avoidance or non-avoidance) of ravine salamanders (Plethodon richmondi) to substrates marked with chemical cues from the tails of autonomized conspecifics. Trials were conducted in 13cm x 2cm glass petri dishes, each dish contained a substrate that was marked with either homogenized tail, autonomized tail, non-injured conspecific or aged water. Salamanders tended to avoid substrates marked with homogenized and autonomized tails and did not avoid substrates marked by non-injured salamanders and aged water. These results suggest that chemical alarm cues can be released from the tails of ravine salamanders and these cues can be detected and avoided.

title: Acoustic competition in male Pelodytes punctatus. Interactive playback experiments

abstract_text: The advertisement call of Pelodytes punctatus is composed of two distinct pulsed notes (A & B). A single A note is always emitted at the beginning of a calling bout and it may be followed by a sequence of 0 to 6 B notes. We designed a playback experiment to mimick the effect of competing male calls with call bouts of different number of Bs on a naturally calling focal male. The A and B notes used in the playback tests were natural calls selected by their overall similarity with a sample of calls of different animals from the same population, measured through audiospectrogram correlations. Tests were performed in the field in southern Portugal with a set up that included an Apple portable computer and interactive playback 'Sound Maker' software (the call of the focal animal triggered the response of the playback sound). When exposed to stimuli with increasing number of B notes, males did not increase the number of B notes in their calls. They did increase call repetition rate. Other static call parameters (duration, frequency and number of pulses of A & B) did not change linearly with number of B notes in the stimulus.

title: Radiotracking amphibians: lessons from implant and external attachment procedures

authors.affiliation: Department of Biological Sciences, State University of New York at Binghamton, Binghamton, New York 13902-6000

abstract_text: Year round radiotracking of Ambystoma maculatum, A. tigrinum, Cryptobranchus alleganiensis, and Rana clamitans has lead to improved package design, surgical procedures, field release and recovery, and positioning techniques. External packages are generally unacceptable for tracking amphibians. Amphibian skin is too physiologically active, delicate and moist for the attachment of external units by waist bands, harnesses, collars, glues or sutures. Packages fixed to the amphibian integument has caused tethering and even injury and death in the animal's struggle to free itself. External packages can also prevent amphibians from entering or turning around in small mammal tunnels, airways, vegetative tangles and rock crevices. External packages, stomach inserts, and surgical (coelomic) implants were used on aquatic hellbenders to test the various methods in a natural setting. The implants worked best, followed by the inserts, which were defecated after 10 days. External packages were unsatisfactory. Radiotransmitter implants were used successfully in all the above species, but precautions with design, implant surgery, and field deployment must be taken. Implant packages should be small enough to allow amphibians to turn around in tight spaces and be coated with beeswax instead of paraffin. Sutures should be more closely spaced in cold weather, and cyanoacrylate should be avoided. Animals should be released at the beginning of their daily activity cycle in the same pulse of ecological/social events from which they were removed. Finally, "local triangulation" should be used to obtain positions; visual fixes should normally be avoided.

title: A laboratory study of foraging behavior in young northern water snakes (Nerodia sipedon): The effect of water depth, habitat structure, and ontogeny on foraging proficiency

abstract_text: I carried out a laboratory study of foraging proficiency in young northern water snakes (Nerodia sipedon) presented with different water depths (0.25, 0.50, 1.00, 2.00 in.), and the presence or absence of artificial habitat structure. Over a seventeen month period and using two litters of young water snakes, I performed three laboratory experiments in which I measured the time required to capture and ingest live minnows in a small feeding arena during 30-minute trials. Snakes generally took less time to capture fish in shallower water than they did in deeper water. Ingestion times largely were unaffected by depth. Larger/older snakes took less time to capture fish than did smaller/young snakes, and larger snakes also captured more fish than did smaller snakes. In an experiment using one litter of young snakes, I found that capture and ingestion times generally were unaffected by the presence of one form of habitat structure, despite its importance as documented in other studies.

title: Comparative behavior of two parthenogenetic and one bisexual species of Cnemidophorus lizards from southern Texas

authors.affiliation: Department of Biological & Environmental Sciences, McNeese State University, Lake Charles, Louisiana 70609, USA

abstract_text: Two species of the all-female, parthenogenetic Cnemidophorus laredoensis complex (Teiidae) coexist with the bisexual species Cnemidophorus gularis in the Rio Grande Valley of southern Texas and northern Mexico. I studied the behavior of the two parthenogenetic species, provisionally designated 'LAR-A' (= C. laredoensis) and 'LAR-B', and C. gularis through focal animal observations of free-ranging lizards in a state park in Texas. Focal animals were followed for a minimum of 10 minutes and all behaviors were recorded into a tape recorder. Playback of the tapes allowed determination of the amount of time lizards spent performing various behaviors. Observations were made during the May to June breeding seasons of 1994-1996. The major differences were between males of C. gularis and LAR-A, LAR-B, and C. gularis females. In general, C. gularis males spent a significantly greater percentage of time interacting with other lizards (most often courting conspecific females or parthenogenetic females), moved greater distances during the time they were observed, and moved faster than C. gularis females and females of the two parthenogenetic species. There were few behavioral differences between C. gularis females and parthenogenetic females. The two parthenogens did devote a greater percentage of their time to searching for food than did C. gularis males and females; however there was no significant difference in the rate of capture of arthropod prey. Overall, the results suggest that the behavioral differences between sexes are greater than the behavioral differences between species in this group of lizards despite differing reproductive modes.

title: Environmental cues used by juvenile corn snakes (Elaphe g. guttata) for spatial learning and memory of an escape task

abstract_text: Spatial orientation is necessary for snake survival, mediating important behaviors such as den localization and predator escape responses. To characterize cues used for spatial orientation, eight juvenile corn snakes were trained to find the only open hole within a circular arena, given a choice of eight holes. During training, snakes showed significant decreases in the latency to find the goal and in the path length taken to find the goal. A significant increase was found in the percent movement in the goal quadrant. Manipulations of controlled environmental cues (rotation of a cue card, rotation of the arena, release from a new position in the arena, and removal of the cue card) were done to examine the effects on orientation to the goal. The results indicate that no one particular cue was used by all of the snakes, although rotation of the cue card and arena affected the most snakes. Individuals were affected differently by different cue manipulations, and some snakes appear to use multiple environmental cues for this task. Snakes also appear to use cues which were not manipulated, such as extra-arena (e.g. overhead lights) and intra-arena cues (e.g. variation in the arena surface).

title: Testing the assumption that satiated salamanders are less likely to risk nocturnal movement

authors.affiliation: Cumberland College, Dept. of Biology, 7196 College Station Drive, Williamsburg, KY 40769, USA

abstract_text: If predation is a serious threat to salamanders, and if predation is more likely when salamanders are moving about at night, away from a place of retreat, then it would seem an unnecessary risk for well fed salamanders to move about as much as those which are having difficulty finding food. Juvenile Plethodon glutinosus, measuring 35-50mm svl, of two feeding groups, 6 in each group, were kept in enclosures where nocturnal movements could be detected by infrared beam interruptions. Enclosures measured 35 x 35cm, were 5cm in height, and a single cover object was provided in the center of each. Small crickets, 6-10mm, were given as food every 5th day within the 20 days of recording. Well fed salamanders ate 4-6 crickets at a feeding and gained mass over the test period. The less well fed salamanders were allowed 1-2 crickets at a feeding and either gained or lost mass minimally. The well fed group demonstrated significantly less movement than the group which ate less (t=4.27, p<0.001). These results are consistent with a view that movements outside of a place of retreat pose a risk for juvenile P. glutinosus.

title: Structural differences in gill vasculature among batoid elasmobranchs

authors.affiliation: Nova Southeastern University Oceanographic Center, 8000 N. Ocean Drive, Dania, FL 33004 USA

abstract_text: Classic studies of gill vasculature indicate the gross anatomy of elasmobranch gills is similar in most species, and in general, resembles those of teleosts. Studies of fine gill structure of several species of batoid elasmobranchs have, however, reported some structural differences. These differences include the presence, in urolophids (Urolophus jamaicensis, U. mucosus, U. paucimaculatus), of 1) a tip channel, possibly an extension of the afferent filament artery that runs along the top of the filament corpus cavernosum, and 2) a vascular arcade, a vessel which connects the afferent filament arteries of a hemibranch near the tip of each filament. To date, these structures were believed to be unique to the urolophids as they were not found in either rajids (Raja erinacea, R. clavata) or the shark Scyliorhinus canicula. Research with the cownose ray (Rhinoptera bonasus) and other batoid elasmobranchs, however, indicates the tip channel and vascular arcade are not unique to urolophids. Additional research is required to determine the phylogenetic and physiologic significances of these structures.

abstract_text: Hyla chrysoscelis, family Hylidae, ranges from Southern Canada south to Texas and Florida. Internal oral morphology and chondrocranial anatomy for this species have not been described. However, chondrocranial data is available for eight species within the family Hylidae. Herein, we describe the internal oral anatomy using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), chondrocranial anatomy, and ossification sequence for H. chrysoscelis. abstract_text: The chondrocranial morphology and skeletogenesis of tadpoles in the genus Physalaemus remains unknown. Herein, we describe the chondrocranial morphology of three species: Physalaemus gracilis, P. henselii, and P. pustulosus. Skeletogenesis is reported based on complete developmental series of P. gracilis and P. pustulosus. Tadpoles were fixed, staged (following Gosner's table, 1960), and cleared and double-stained for cartilage and bone using standard procedures. Examination of the whole-mounted and stained specimens revealed little difference in chondrocranial anatomy and the onset of ossification among the three species. Physalaemus is characterized by having suprarostrals in which the ala and the corpus are fused dorsally. Furthermore the suprarostrals are ventromedially fused. Physalaemus also exhibits a well-developed processus quadratoethmoidalis. A processus pseudopterygoideus is present only in P. gracilis. The processus antorbitalis fuses to the tip of the processus muscularis in P. pustulosus and P. henselii to form a commisura quadratoorbitalis, this connection is lacking in P. gracilis. The frontoparietal fenestra of P. pustulosus and P. gracilis is completely divided by well-developed taeni tectum transversalis and taeni tectum medialis, these taenia are absent in P. henselii. A larval otic process is absent and the processus ascendens has an intermediate attachment to the braincase in all three species

title: Development of the suprarostral plate in pipoid frogs

abstract_text: The ethmoid plate of anuran larvae is formed by the fusion of the trabecular and parachordal cartilages early in development. From the antero-lateral edges of this plate, the cornua trabeculae arise as two separate and anteriorly diverging projections. Usually, at their most anterior tips, the cornua trabeculae articulate with the suprarostral cartilages, the element supporting the upper jaw. Modification of the cornua has been demonstrated in several taxa (Wild 1996). In pipids, cornua trabeculae and suprarostral cartilages are not identifiable as separate elements even in relatively early larvae (Nieuwkoop and Faber stage 50). Instead, a single and continuous cartilaginous plate covers the entire area, the suprarostral plate (Trueb and Hanken 1993). This plate has been reported in Xenopus, Pipa, and Rhinophrynus. Hymenochirus boettgeri lacks a suprarostral plate and possesses a further modified ethmoid area. Tadpoles of Xenopus laevis, Rhinophrynus dorsalis and Hymenochirus boettgeri were studied using whole-mounted cleared and stained specimens and paraffin and plastic embedded cross-sectioned material. Herein we describe the development of the suprarostral plate in Xenopus laevis, Rhinophrynus dorsalis with comments on the condition in Hymenochirus boettgeri

title: Ultrastructure of gymnophione scales and their utility as phylogenetic characters

authors.affiliation: Natural History Museum and Department of Systematics and Ecology, The University of Kansas USA

abstract_text: Since Taylor's Atlas of Scales (1972), interspecific variation among caecilian scales has been virtually ignored, and only the presence or absence of scales has been used as a phylogenetic character. The issue of variation has focused on scale morphology within and among individuals of a single species. Considerable variation has been found in the size, shape, arrangement, and number of scales, and thus, scales have been regarded as too variable to be phylogenetically informative. The surface morphology of scales has been investigated in detail in only a few taxa. The outer-most layer of caecilian scales is comprised of mineralized squamulae. The objectives of this study were to investigate intraspecific and interspecific variation in the arrangement and shape of the squamulae, and to address whether there are scale characteristics, besides the presence or absence of scales, that can be utilized in reconstructing phylogenies. Scales from representative of the four caecilian families that possess scales were removed and analyzed using light and scanning electron microscopy. Little intraspecific variation was found in scale ultrastructure, while a good deal of interspecific variation was identified. Variation in scale ultrastructure among taxa is quantified and scale characters are discussed.

abstract_text: The development of the supraorbital and mandibular canals was analyzed in Archocentrus nigrofasciatus (n=26, 4.5-11.5 mm SL) in order to evaluate conflicting descriptions of canal morphogenesis and the manner in which they are incorporated into dermal cranial bones. Neuromasts of the dorsal aspect of the head were examined (n=6, 4.5 - 8.0 mm SL) using SEM to clarify their identity as presumptive canal or superficial neuromasts. Four developmental stages were identified. Neuromasts arise in the epithelium (Stage I) and a bony plate ossifies under each neuromast. In addition, regression analyses reveal that neuromast width and canal width exhibit a positive linear relationship with fish size in both the supraorbital and mandibular canals indicating that there are probably ongoing interactions between neuromasts and dermal bones after initial canal ossification.

title: Lessons from E.J. Crossman - The relevance of a comprehensive approach to fish taxonomy

abstract_text: In his direction to students, Dr. E.J. Crossman emphasizes and encourages a comprehensive approach to questions and problems of fish systematic and taxonomic studies which, at the time I was doing my degree work, were dominated by morphological and osetological approaches. Recently such studies have become dominated by genetic approaches which often rely solely upon tissues provided to laboratories rather than the fish themselves, and focus solely upon variation at the molecular level. Little or no reference is usually made to other character systems such as morphology, osteology, ecology or biology. For well known groups and studies at higher taxonomic levels this bias may not matter, and genetic studies add another dimension to our knowledge. However, for poorly known groups and lower taxonomic levels, working solely with tissues can limit understanding, may bias results, and result in erroneous conclusions. External morphology is often the first clue to undiscovered diversity. Genetic variation may be present but without associated knowledge of morphology may not be interpreted correctly. Thus, quantifying and understanding morphological diversity is important in the development of hypotheses which can then be tested using other approaches such as genetics. Morphological diversity within an esociform (Olympic mudminnow, Novumbra hubbsi) and morphological and genetic diversity within a salmoniform group (Arctic and Dolly Varden chars, Salvelinus spp.) are used to illustrate the need for close association of various approaches to achieve fuller understanding of diversity and relationships of fishes. abstract_text: In the absence of bone marrow and lymph nodes, elasmobranch fish must rely on alternative lymphomyeloid tissues for production of immune cells. abstract_text: In most elasmobranchs, growth of vertebral cartilage proceeds incrementally and forms periodic marks that are extensively used in age and growth studies. Finally, the effect of parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHrp) on GAG synthesis was examined, because of its critical role in mammalian skeletogenesis. PTHrp has recently been detected in the perichondrium of elasmobranch vertebral cartilage, thus it may play a role in chondrocyte proliferation and differentiation. title: Mechanics of ventilation in the swellshark, Cephaloscyllium ventriosum (Scyliorhinidae)

abstract_text: Most fishes are faced with one of two options for gill ventilation: physically moving their gills through the medium ("ram" ventilation), or actively pumping the medium over their gills via "buccal pumping". The basic pattern of mechanical movements during buccal pumping was studied over 40 years ago. However, unique patterns of water flow through the head of the swellshark during feeding suggested that the generation of respiratory currents might not be as simple as once thought. Using pressure transducers implanted into the buccal and gill cavities of actively respiring swellsharks, it was discovered that pressure traces vary within and among individuals. These data, combined with both video and electrical impedance data for the displacement of the lower jaw and gill septum, suggest that although the classic pattern of pressure generation regularly occurs, at least one novel pattern of pressure generation exists. During this novel pattern, pressure reversals exist over a much longer duration than previously thought possible, and at much larger magnitudes. It is questionable whether the classic alternating "suction" and "pressure" pumps are always used for moving water over the gills unidirectionally, and whether continuous water flow over the gills exists for large intervals of time in this species.

abstract_text: The swell shark, Cephaloscyllium ventriosum, is an oviparous chondrichthyan fish. Each egg capsule contains a single embryo that is incubated on the sea floor for 7.5 to 10 months. The horny capsule material is not sufficiently permeable to oxygen to supply the needs of a late stage embryo, however, after about one third of development four slits open in the sides of the egg case to admit seawater. Early stage embryos have a relatively large tail appendage that is used to generate a water current through the capsule.
